architectural_implications.after: Sandbox holds no secrets; an identity-aware layer injects the calling user's credentials per HTTP/SQL call.
architectural_implications.before: Secrets stored in the sandbox; any process or agent with sandbox access inherits their full authority.
architectural_implications.consequence: Authorization becomes per-request and identity-derived, collapsing the escalation path from low-privilege agent to high-privilege action, at the cost of needing a mediating proxy for every tool/data call.
architectural_implications.observation: Credentials are currently colocated with agent execution (secrets inside the cloud code sandbox).

architectural_implications.after: One company-wide wiki where each page carries deterministic, user-controlled scopes and human attribution.
architectural_implications.before: Memory siloed per team (Slack channel memory), unshareable globally.
architectural_implications.consequence: A single retrieval surface can serve mixed-privilege collaborators (e.g., incident response) while enforcement moves to page-level grants.
architectural_implications.observation: Shared agent context is partitioned by team/channel rather than by artifact scope.

architectural_implications.after: Agents propose scoped additions that require human confirmation before merge.
architectural_implications.before: Agents auto-add memory/wiki pages; provenance is untracked.
architectural_implications.consequence: Knowledge ingestion becomes a reviewed pipeline rather than an open write path, adding latency and human effort but producing attributable, auditable context.
architectural_implications.observation: Agent memory writes go directly into the store.

article_ideas.angle: Take the talk's four-rule architecture at face value, then stress it: enumerate how an identity-injecting HTTP/SQL layer can be induced to act on behalf of the wrong principal, and specify the invariants (call-bound identity binding, no token passthrough, per-call scope derivation) that must hold for the claim to be true.
article_ideas.audience: Enterprise security architects and platform engineers deploying agents inside regulated networks
article_ideas.based_on: treat the sandbox as untrusted compute and move credential resolution to an identity-aware proxy layer
article_ideas.thesis: Pulling secrets out of the agent's code sandbox and injecting them per-request from the caller's identity is the right default, but it converts a static privilege-escalation bug into a confused-deputy problem at the injection layer — so the article argues the mediation proxy, not the sandbox, is where the security budget belongs.
article_ideas.title: Your sandbox is not your trust boundary: credential virtualization moves the blast radius, it doesn't remove it

article_ideas.angle: Contrast the three sharing patterns the talk rejects (shared skills repo, per-team channel memory, auto-write) against the shared-wiki-with-scopes model, and argue that the design's viability is a function of enforcement placement rather than of retrieval quality.
article_ideas.audience: AI platform leads and engineers designing agent memory and RAG systems for mixed-privilege organizations
article_ideas.based_on: access control lives on context artifacts rather than on separate per-team stores
article_ideas.thesis: Centralized retrieval plus artifact-level scopes beats per-team memory silos and shared skills repos — but only if scope enforcement is provable at context-assembly time, because centralizing context converts every scope bug from a local leak into a company-wide one.
article_ideas.title: One brain, many privilege levels: put the partition key on the artifact, not on the team

article_ideas.angle: Treat agent memory ingestion as a code-review problem: define override rate, review latency, and the point at which human confirmation becomes nominal, then argue that any design that skips the staging step is optimizing for a metric (update volume) it will later regret.
article_ideas.audience: Engineers and engineering managers building internal knowledge and agent-memory tooling
article_ideas.based_on: Write paths to shared agent memory should be staged (propose → human confirm → merge)
article_ideas.thesis: The propose-scope-confirm-merge pipeline is the load-bearing part of a company brain, and its review throughput — not its retrieval quality — is what determines whether the brain stays attributable as it grows.
article_ideas.title: Agents as contributors, not committers: the write path is the product

article_ideas.angle: Reframe the enterprise agent roadmap around the review artifacts a security team actually asks for — deterministic scopes, human attribution, credential isolation, reviewable write paths — and argue that capability-first roadmaps are solving for the wrong buyer.
article_ideas.audience: Founders and product leads selling agent infrastructure into regulated enterprises
article_ideas.based_on: security questionnaires are the actual deployment gate
article_ideas.thesis: In banks and Fortune 100 environments the deployment gate is provable containment of privilege, not agent capability, so agent infrastructure that makes escalation structurally impossible will outcompete more capable tooling on those accounts.
article_ideas.title: The security questionnaire is the real benchmark: why containment beats capability in regulated agent adoption

connections.connects_to: retrieval-time access control in RAG/agent memory
connections.relationship: Scopes are the partitioning key that lets a single retrieval index serve multiple privilege levels; enforcement must occur where context is assembled, not only where it is stored.

connections.concept: credential virtualization at the HTTP/SQL layer
connections.relationship: Moving secrets out of the sandbox relocates the trust boundary from the execution environment to an identity-aware mediation layer.
Distributed authorship requires a review/confirmation pipeline to keep quality and attribution; the two mechanisms are interdependent.
Isolated per-team memory reproduces the same information-partitioning problem that multi-agent systems face when agents cannot share context.
Compliance review, not benchmark performance, is the operative filter for whether agent infrastructure is permitted inside regulated networks.

evidence_quotes.text: Do not store credentials in the cloud sandbox
Inject user credentials at the HTTP/SQL layer dynamically based on the initiating user's identity
storing shared credentials in the sandbox lets low-privilege agents execute high-privilege actions

core_insights.generalization: Applies to any agent runtime with tool/network access: treat the sandbox as untrusted compute and move credential resolution to an identity-aware proxy layer in front of tools and data.
core_insights.insight: Credential virtualization: rather than storing API keys or DB credentials in the agent's cloud code sandbox, inject the initiating user's credentials dynamically at the HTTP/SQL layer so the agent's effective privileges are bounded by the requesting user's identity, not the sandbox's contents.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This removes the privilege-escalation path where a low-privilege agent or user can execute high-privilege actions simply by reaching shared secrets inside the execution environment. It converts authorization from a static artifact (stored secret) into a per-call, identity-derived decision.

evidence_quotes.text: Wiki pages can have scopes that users can control deterministically
All context goes into a company-wide wiki and must have a human's name attached
deterministic scopes and human attribution

core_insights.generalization: Context stores for agents can be centralized for retrieval quality while remaining partitioned at the artifact level; the partition key belongs on the memory object, not on the retrieval index or the agent.
core_insights.insight: Human attribution plus explicit, user-controlled scopes on each wiki page is the enforcement mechanism that lets one shared knowledge store serve many privilege levels — access control lives on context artifacts rather than on separate per-team stores.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It is the design that resolves the apparent conflict between 'one company-wide brain' and 'interns must not see secrets'. Scopes are deterministic and user-declared, so auditing is straightforward and escalation is bounded by page-level grants.

evidence_quotes.text: Agents should not auto-add memory or wiki pages without human confirmation
Require agents to suggest additions with scopes, requiring human confirmation before merging into the wiki
Allowing agents to auto-write leads to untracked changes where nobody knows who added sensitive details

core_insights.generalization: Write paths to shared agent memory should be staged (propose → human confirm → merge), analogous to code review, not direct-write.
core_insights.insight: Agents should propose memory/wiki writes with scope annotations but never auto-commit them; human confirmation is required before merge.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It blocks the failure mode where sensitive or low-quality context enters the shared brain with no accountable owner, while still capturing agent-generated suggestions that would otherwise be lost.

evidence_quotes.text: This fails because people do not have time to write skills for others
Keep memory per team (e.g., Slack channel memory). This creates another isolated silo
Claude Tag introducing team channel memory, resulting in siloed data that cannot be shared globally

core_insights.generalization: Collaborative knowledge substrates tend to fail on contribution economics (who pays the writing cost) and on partitioning (silo formation); designs must address both simultaneously.
core_insights.insight: Both common sharing patterns fail for structural reasons, not effort reasons: a shared GitHub skills repo fails because people lack time to write skills for others, and per-team memory (e.g., Slack channel memory) simply relocates the silo. Only a single shared wiki with deterministic scopes and human attribution is claimed to scale.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It argues that 'shared context' cannot be achieved by asking individuals to author for others nor by isolating memory per team — the mechanism must be a shared store with machine-checkable partitioning.

evidence_quotes.text: Organizations that are 100 years old cannot top-down engineer a complete company brain; it must emerge from individual contributions
Grow, don't build, a company brain
Wiki contributions per day increasing steadily from 0 to over 300 updates per day over a two-month period

core_insights.generalization: Knowledge systems that require centralized authoring throttle at the bottleneck's throughput; systems that distribute authorship scale with headcount but need lightweight governance to keep quality.
core_insights.insight: A company brain cannot be built top-down; it must be grown via per-person, self-service contributions that compound — a healthy brain shows monotonically increasing daily update volume.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It reframes the build task from a one-time architecture deliverable into an ongoing contribution-and-stewardship system, implying the tooling must optimize for low-friction individual authoring rather than centralized curation.

evidence_quotes.text: Fear of leaks is the biggest barrier preventing companies from deploying open-source AI tools like OpenClaw or Hermes broadly
Banks and Fortune 100 companies have strict security rules against vibe-coded AI agents running inside their networks
security questionnaire

core_insights.generalization: Adoption of agentic tooling in regulated environments is bottlenecked by provable containment of privilege, so infrastructure that makes privilege non-escalable will outcompete capability-focused tooling there.
core_insights.insight: Security fear of leaks — not capability — is the gating factor for enterprise adoption of open-source agent tooling, and banks/Fortune 100 specifically prohibit 'vibe-coded' agents from running inside their networks.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It implies the near-term enterprise market demand is for isolation, deterministic scoping, and auditability of agents rather than more agent capability, and that security questionnaires are the actual deployment gate.

evidence_quotes.text: Wiki pages can have scopes that users can control deterministically
All context goes into a company-wide wiki and must have a human's name attached
deterministic scopes and human attribution

deep_dives.research_question: If a wiki page carries deterministic user-controlled scopes, at which point must filtering occur so that the page is provably absent from a lower-privilege user's context — including through summarization, embedding retrieval, and cached derived artifacts?
deep_dives.topic: Scope enforcement placement: index-time vs. query-time filtering and derived-artifact leakage
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Wiki pages can have scopes that users can control deterministically
deep_dives.why: The entire 'one shared brain for many privilege levels' design rests on scope enforcement being deterministic. If scopes are enforced only at storage or only at the top-k retrieval step, a low-privilege caller can still reconstruct protected content through summaries, embeddings, or cross-page inference — turning the single shared store into a broad leak surface instead of a local one.

evidence_quotes.text: Do not store credentials in the cloud sandbox
storing shared credentials in the sandbox lets low-privilege agents execute high-privilege actions

deep_dives.research_question: What is the blast radius and failure mode set of an identity-aware layer that injects the initiating user's credentials per HTTP/SQL call — and can a low-privilege caller induce it to make a high-privilege call through confused-deputy, token passthrough, or scope-confusion patterns?
deep_dives.topic: Attack surface of the credential-virtualizing proxy (confused deputy, SSRF, scope confusion)
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Inject user credentials at the HTTP/SQL layer dynamically based on the initiating user's identity
deep_dives.why: Credential virtualization is presented as the fix, but it relocates trust from the sandbox to a new mediation component that sits on every tool and data call. If that component can be confused about who initiated a call, the escalation path returns in a subtler form, and the fix becomes the vulnerable asset.

evidence_quotes.text: Agents should not auto-add memory or wiki pages without human confirmation
Require agents to suggest additions with scopes, requiring human confirmation before merging into the wiki
Allowing agents to auto-write leads to untracked changes where nobody knows who added sensitive details

deep_dives.research_question: As wiki update volume scales toward hundreds of updates per day, does human confirmation of agent-proposed, scoped additions remain a real review step, or does it degrade into rubber-stamping with rising auto-approval and override-reversal rates?
deep_dives.topic: Review economics of the propose-then-confirm memory write path under high update volume
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Agents should not auto-add memory or wiki pages without human confirmation
deep_dives.why: The write path is the only mechanism preventing unattributable or sensitive context from entering the brain. Its throughput limit, not its design, determines whether it survives contact with a growing brain — and a rubber-stamped review pipeline is functionally equivalent to the auto-write path it was meant to replace.

evidence_quotes.text: Wiki contributions per day increasing steadily from 0 to over 300 updates per day over a two-month period
Grow, don't build, a company brain
Organizations that are 100 years old cannot top-down engineer a complete company brain; it must emerge from individual contributions

deep_dives.research_question: Does an increasing daily wiki update rate correlate with downstream retrieval quality and agent task success, or does it mainly track duplication, churn, and low-value edits?
deep_dives.topic: Is rising daily update volume a health metric or a noise metric?
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Wiki contributions per day increasing steadily from 0 to over 300 updates per day over a two-month period
deep_dives.why: 'Healthy company brain' is operationalized in the talk as a monotonic rise in contributions per day. If that metric is uncorrelated with task outcomes, organizations will optimize a vanity counter while their context store degrades in precision, poisoning agent behavior at scale.

project_ideas.measurement: Leakage rate (recovered protected facts per 100 queries) per filter placement and per probe type, plus the false-exclusion rate showing how much legitimate context index-time partitioning costs.
project_ideas.name: Scope-Leak Harness
project_ideas.poc: Build a synthetic company wiki with tiered-scope pages, two retrieval modes (index-time partition vs. query-time filter), and three leak probes: top-k direct retrieval, summarization over mixed-privilege results, and nearest-neighbor reconstruction from embedding indexes; run each probe as a low-privilege caller and attempt to recover protected facts.

project_ideas.based_on: Inject user credentials at the HTTP/SQL layer dynamically based on the initiating user's identity
project_ideas.hypothesis: An identity-aware credential-injecting proxy in front of HTTP/SQL tools can be induced to execute a call with a higher privilege than the initiating caller's identity in at least one of three patterns: replayed session binding, nested tool call inheriting the prior caller, or scope-confusion in a mediated call whose target is attacker-influenced.
project_ideas.measurement: Number of adversarial traces producing a successful high-privilege call, classified by pattern, and the minimum proxy hardening change that drives each pattern to zero.
project_ideas.name: Confused-Deputy Injection Proxy Red Team
project_ideas.poc: Stand up a minimal injection proxy that resolves credentials per call from a caller identity token, wrap a mock high-privilege data API behind it, and run a suite of adversarial agent traces (prompt-injected nested calls, session-replay, target-rewrite) against it.

project_ideas.based_on: Agents should not auto-add memory or wiki pages without human confirmation
project_ideas.hypothesis: At sustained volume above roughly 100 agent-proposed memory additions per day, human confirmation of scoped wiki additions degrades measurably — reviewer dwell time collapses and the unreviewed-or-auto-approved merge fraction rises — even though the pipeline's stated design requires genuine confirmation.
project_ideas.measurement: Median review dwell time, edits-per-merge, rejection rate, and the slope of auto-approval as a function of daily proposal volume; flag the volume at which dwell time drops below a threshold indicating nominal review.
project_ideas.name: Review-at-Scale Memory Pipeline
project_ideas.poc: Instrument a propose-scope-confirm-merge pipeline with synthetic but realistic agent suggestions at 10, 50, 150 and 300 additions/day, recording dwell time, edit-before-merge rate, and rejection rate per volume tier.

project_ideas.based_on: Wiki contributions per day increasing steadily from 0 to over 300 updates per day over a two-month period
project_ideas.hypothesis: Rising daily wiki update volume is a noisy proxy for brain health: above some threshold, marginal updates correlate with duplication and contradiction in the context store and with flat or declining agent task success, not with improved success.
project_ideas.measurement: Correlation between weekly update volume and agent task success rate, plus duplication and contradiction density in the store; report whether success improves, plateaus, or degrades past a volume inflection.
project_ideas.name: Update-Rate vs. Task-Outcome Study
project_ideas.poc: Run a longitudinal instrumented deployment (or a simulated one seeded with the reported 0-to-300+ updates/day trajectory) that logs update rate alongside context-store duplication/contradiction metrics and a fixed agent task suite's success and error rates.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Tanmai Gopal
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Security and architecture of company brains and AI agents in enterprise
  • Purpose: To provide enterprise AI engineers with an architectural blueprint for securely building and growing a company brain without leaking sensitive secrets or credentials. Tanmai Gopal, CEO and co-founder of PromptQL, discusses the risks of deploying 'company brains' and open-source AI tools across organizations. He outlines the security risks of sharing company secrets, the failure modes of team-based or agent-based knowledge silos, and proposes a four-rule architecture using a company-wide wiki with deterministic scope enforcement, sandboxing, and virtualized user credentials to prevent data leaks while enabling collaborative AI workflows.

Topic Map

The Company Brain Dilemma and Fear of Leaks

  • Explanation: Companies want a centralized 'company brain' to power AI agents across teams, but fear that interns or bad actors will access sensitive company secrets.
  • Key claims:
    • Building a company brain risks leaking company secrets.
    • Fear of leaks is the biggest barrier preventing companies from deploying open-source AI tools like OpenClaw or Hermes broadly.
    • Banks and Fortune 100 companies have strict security rules against vibe-coded AI agents running inside their networks.
  • Examples:
    • An intern joining a company and immediately gaining access to competitor details and sensitive company information.
  • Terminology:
    • company brain
    • OpenClaw
    • Hermes
    • vibe-coded AI agents
  • Why it matters: Security concerns block enterprises from adopting powerful AI agents and shared knowledge bases.

Growth Dynamics of a Healthy Company Brain

  • Explanation: Analyzing the contribution history and update frequency of a healthy company-wide wiki or brain over time.
  • Key claims:
    • A healthy company brain scales in size and experiences an increasing number of daily updates per day.
    • When AI agents and teams start working successfully, people continuously teach the system new skills, interpretations, and actions.
    • Systemic learning rates compound as users add querying, interpretation, action, and A/B testing skills.
  • Examples:
    • Wiki contributions per day increasing steadily from 0 to over 300 updates per day over a two-month period.
  • Terminology:
    • shared context
    • wiki contributions
    • auto-learning
    • stewardship
  • Why it matters: Understanding how healthy knowledge graphs evolve helps organizations architect sustainable feedback loops.

Use Cases: Company AI and Collaborative Incident Management

  • Explanation: Exploring how company brains are used either as a shared context for individual AI agents or as a collaborative workspace for teams.
  • Key claims:
    • Use Case 1: Individual AI agents querying the company brain to get work done using existing company knowledge and skills.
    • Use Case 2: Collaborative incident management where multiple team members with different privilege levels collaborate via shared AI context.
    • Both use cases present significant security and escalation challenges.
  • Examples:
    • An engineer fetching logs, investigating codebases, raising a PR, setting up alerts, and deploying to production collaboratively with AI.
  • Terminology:
    • security questionnaire
    • collaborative incident management
    • escalation levels
    • privilege levels
  • Why it matters: Different use cases require distinct security boundaries between personal context, team context, and company-wide knowledge.

Three Architectural Options for Company Brains

  • Explanation: Evaluating three architectural approaches for managing shared skills and memory: GitHub repos, team silos, and company-wide wikis.
  • Key claims:
    • Option 1: Everybody writes shared skills on GitHub. This fails because people do not have time to write skills for others.
    • Option 2: Keep memory per team (e.g., Slack channel memory). This creates another isolated silo.
    • Option 3: All context goes into a single shared wiki with deterministic scopes and human attribution.
  • Examples:
    • Claude Tag introducing team channel memory, resulting in siloed data that cannot be shared globally.
  • Terminology:
    • GitHub repo
    • team silos
    • shared wiki
    • scopes
  • Why it matters: Choosing the right architecture prevents data silos and unmanageable credential escalation.

The Four Rules for a Secure Company Brain

  • Explanation: Laying down four concrete design rules for building a secure company brain with company AI.
  • Key claims:
    • Rule 1: All context goes into a company-wide wiki and must have a human's name attached.
    • Rule 2: Wiki pages can have scopes that users can control deterministically.
    • Rule 3: Do not store credentials in the cloud sandbox.
    • Rule 4: Virtualize tool and data calls to inject user credentials dynamically so users control access.
  • Examples:
    • Adding context to a wiki page with explicit finance or personal scopes, reviewed and confirmed by a human.
  • Terminology:
    • company-wide wiki
    • scopes
    • cloud sandbox
    • credential virtualization
  • Why it matters: Following these four rules ensures high-quality context without privilege escalation or secret leakage.

Key Points

Grow, don't build, a company brain

  • Explanation: Companies cannot build a massive company brain top-down; instead, each person must own and build their own piece of the company brain incrementally.
  • Evidence: Organizations that are 100 years old cannot top-down engineer a complete company brain; it must emerge from individual contributions.
  • Practical implication: Empower every employee to contribute context and skills self-service while maintaining personal responsibility for security.

Prevent automatic agent memory writes

  • Explanation: Agents should not auto-add memory or wiki pages without human confirmation, as this leads to unverified, low-quality, or leaking context.
  • Evidence: Allowing agents to auto-write leads to untracked changes where nobody knows who added sensitive details.
  • Practical implication: Require agents to suggest additions with scopes, requiring human confirmation before merging into the wiki.

Never store credentials in the code sandbox

  • Explanation: Storing API keys or database credentials inside the cloud code sandbox allows any agent or user with access to execute unauthorized tools.
  • Evidence: If an engineer can merge PRs and an SRE manager can deploy to production, storing shared credentials in the sandbox lets low-privilege agents execute high-privilege actions.
  • Practical implication: Inject user credentials at the HTTP/SQL layer dynamically based on the initiating user's identity.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Four Rules for a Secure Company Brain

  • How it works: Combines a centralized wiki structure with human attribution, deterministic scope controls, sandboxed execution, and dynamic credential virtualization.
  • Components:
    • Company-wide wiki with human name attribution
    • Deterministic read/write access scopes on wiki pages
    • Zero credential storage in cloud sandboxes
    • Virtualized tool and data calls injecting user credentials
  • When to use: When deploying enterprise AI agents or company brains across multi-tier teams and regulated industries.

Examples & Case Studies

An engineer investigating an auto-learning bug noticed wiki pages failing due to prefix mismatches in integration wiki titles.

  • Illustrates: How team conversations and debugging discussions create high-quality context when documented correctly.
  • Lesson: Interactive debugging threads generate valuable tribal knowledge that should be vetted and added to the company wiki with human sign-off.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Stop letting AI agents automatically commit memory without human review.
    • Attach human names to every piece of knowledge added to shared company wikis.
  • Strategic:
    • Shift from team-isolated silos to a single company-wide wiki with deterministic scopes.
    • Separate agent execution sandboxes from actual user credentials by virtualizing data and tool calls.
  • Questions to investigate:

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Most developers will not write shared skills for other people in GitHub repos. (empirical observation)
  • Injecting user credentials at the HTTP and SQL layer prevents privilege escalation in shared AI agents. (architectural principle)

Notable Quotes

"Your company brain will leak company secrets." "We're going to grow a company brain. Not build one."

Compressed Summary

  • Company brains risk leaking enterprise secrets if not architected with strict access controls.
  • Option 3 wiki architecture with human attribution and scopes outperforms GitHub repos and team silos.
  • Never store credentials in cloud code sandboxes.
  • Virtualize tool and data calls to inject user credentials dynamically during execution.
  • Keywords: company brain, security, wiki, credentials, virtualization
  • Core insight: Securing a company brain requires combining a human-attributed, scoped shared wiki with dynamic credential injection at the data layer instead of storing keys in agent sandboxes.

## Topic Map
### The Company Brain Dilemma and Fear of Leaks
- **Explanation**: Companies want a centralized 'company brain' to power AI agents across teams, but fear that interns or bad actors will access sensitive company secrets.
- **Key claims**:
  - Building a company brain risks leaking company secrets.
  - Fear of leaks is the biggest barrier preventing companies from deploying open-source AI tools like OpenClaw or Hermes broadly.
  - Banks and Fortune 100 companies have strict security rules against vibe-coded AI agents running inside their networks.
- **Examples**:
  - An intern joining a company and immediately gaining access to competitor details and sensitive company information.
- **Terminology**:
  - company brain
  - OpenClaw
  - Hermes
  - vibe-coded AI agents
- **Why it matters**: Security concerns block enterprises from adopting powerful AI agents and shared knowledge bases.
### Growth Dynamics of a Healthy Company Brain
- **Explanation**: Analyzing the contribution history and update frequency of a healthy company-wide wiki or brain over time.
- **Key claims**:
  - A healthy company brain scales in size and experiences an increasing number of daily updates per day.
  - When AI agents and teams start working successfully, people continuously teach the system new skills, interpretations, and actions.
  - Systemic learning rates compound as users add querying, interpretation, action, and A/B testing skills.
- **Examples**:
  - Wiki contributions per day increasing steadily from 0 to over 300 updates per day over a two-month period.
- **Terminology**:
  - shared context
  - wiki contributions
  - auto-learning
  - stewardship
- **Why it matters**: Understanding how healthy knowledge graphs evolve helps organizations architect sustainable feedback loops.
### Use Cases: Company AI and Collaborative Incident Management
- **Explanation**: Exploring how company brains are used either as a shared context for individual AI agents or as a collaborative workspace for teams.
- **Key claims**:
  - Use Case 1: Individual AI agents querying the company brain to get work done using existing company knowledge and skills.
  - Use Case 2: Collaborative incident management where multiple team members with different privilege levels collaborate via shared AI context.
  - Both use cases present significant security and escalation challenges.
- **Examples**:
  - An engineer fetching logs, investigating codebases, raising a PR, setting up alerts, and deploying to production collaboratively with AI.
- **Terminology**:
  - security questionnaire
  - collaborative incident management
  - escalation levels
  - privilege levels
- **Why it matters**: Different use cases require distinct security boundaries between personal context, team context, and company-wide knowledge.
### Three Architectural Options for Company Brains
- **Explanation**: Evaluating three architectural approaches for managing shared skills and memory: GitHub repos, team silos, and company-wide wikis.
- **Key claims**:
  - Option 1: Everybody writes shared skills on GitHub. This fails because people do not have time to write skills for others.
  - Option 2: Keep memory per team (e.g., Slack channel memory). This creates another isolated silo.
  - Option 3: All context goes into a single shared wiki with deterministic scopes and human attribution.
- **Examples**:
  - Claude Tag introducing team channel memory, resulting in siloed data that cannot be shared globally.
- **Terminology**:
  - GitHub repo
  - team silos
  - shared wiki
  - scopes
- **Why it matters**: Choosing the right architecture prevents data silos and unmanageable credential escalation.
### The Four Rules for a Secure Company Brain
- **Explanation**: Laying down four concrete design rules for building a secure company brain with company AI.
- **Key claims**:
  - Rule 1: All context goes into a company-wide wiki and must have a human's name attached.
  - Rule 2: Wiki pages can have scopes that users can control deterministically.
  - Rule 3: Do not store credentials in the cloud sandbox.
  - Rule 4: Virtualize tool and data calls to inject user credentials dynamically so users control access.
- **Examples**:
  - Adding context to a wiki page with explicit finance or personal scopes, reviewed and confirmed by a human.
- **Terminology**:
  - company-wide wiki
  - scopes
  - cloud sandbox
  - credential virtualization
- **Why it matters**: Following these four rules ensures high-quality context without privilege escalation or secret leakage.
## Key Points
### Grow, don't build, a company brain
- **Explanation**: Companies cannot build a massive company brain top-down; instead, each person must own and build their own piece of the company brain incrementally.
- **Evidence**: Organizations that are 100 years old cannot top-down engineer a complete company brain; it must emerge from individual contributions.
- **Practical implication**: Empower every employee to contribute context and skills self-service while maintaining personal responsibility for security.
### Prevent automatic agent memory writes
- **Explanation**: Agents should not auto-add memory or wiki pages without human confirmation, as this leads to unverified, low-quality, or leaking context.
- **Evidence**: Allowing agents to auto-write leads to untracked changes where nobody knows who added sensitive details.
- **Practical implication**: Require agents to suggest additions with scopes, requiring human confirmation before merging into the wiki.
### Never store credentials in the code sandbox
- **Explanation**: Storing API keys or database credentials inside the cloud code sandbox allows any agent or user with access to execute unauthorized tools.
- **Evidence**: If an engineer can merge PRs and an SRE manager can deploy to production, storing shared credentials in the sandbox lets low-privilege agents execute high-privilege actions.
- **Practical implication**: Inject user credentials at the HTTP/SQL layer dynamically based on the initiating user's identity.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Four Rules for a Secure Company Brain
- **How it works**: Combines a centralized wiki structure with human attribution, deterministic scope controls, sandboxed execution, and dynamic credential virtualization.
- **Components**:
  - Company-wide wiki with human name attribution
  - Deterministic read/write access scopes on wiki pages
  - Zero credential storage in cloud sandboxes
  - Virtualized tool and data calls injecting user credentials
- **When to use**: When deploying enterprise AI agents or company brains across multi-tier teams and regulated industries.
## Examples & Case Studies
### An engineer investigating an auto-learning bug noticed wiki pages failing due to prefix mismatches in integration wiki titles.
- **Illustrates**: How team conversations and debugging discussions create high-quality context when documented correctly.
- **Lesson**: Interactive debugging threads generate valuable tribal knowledge that should be vetted and added to the company wiki with human sign-off.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Stop letting AI agents automatically commit memory without human review.
  - Attach human names to every piece of knowledge added to shared company wikis.
- **Strategic**:
  - Shift from team-isolated silos to a single company-wide wiki with deterministic scopes.
  - Separate agent execution sandboxes from actual user credentials by virtualizing data and tool calls.

## Claims Worth Verifying
- Most developers will not write shared skills for other people in GitHub repos. (empirical observation)
- Injecting user credentials at the HTTP and SQL layer prevents privilege escalation in shared AI agents. (architectural principle)
## Notable Quotes
> "Your company brain will leak company secrets."
> "We're going to grow a company brain. Not build one."
## Compressed Summary
- Company brains risk leaking enterprise secrets if not architected with strict access controls.
- Option 3 wiki architecture with human attribution and scopes outperforms GitHub repos and team silos.
- Never store credentials in cloud code sandboxes.
- Virtualize tool and data calls to inject user credentials dynamically during execution.
- **Keywords**: company brain, security, wiki, credentials, virtualization
- **Core insight**: Securing a company brain requires combining a human-attributed, scoped shared wiki with dynamic credential injection at the data layer instead of storing keys in agent sandboxes.
